clinicalPearls: It is the commonest specific dermatosis of pregnancy, accounting for around half of cases.
An umbrella term encompassing eczematous (E-type) and papular (P-type) presentations, and it subsumes the older labels prurigo of pregnancy and pruritic folliculitis of pregnancy.
Characteristically has an early onset, with the majority of cases starting before the third trimester.
Most women have no prior eczema; many experience their first atopic flare during pregnancy, though a personal or family history of atopy is common.
E-type disease shows widespread eczematous change favouring flexures, face, neck and hands; P-type shows disseminated small papules or prurigo-like nodules.
Diagnosis is clinical with negative direct immunofluorescence; total serum IgE is elevated in a substantial proportion.
It carries no maternal or fetal risk but tends to recur in future pregnancies.
Managed with emollients, topical corticosteroids, antihistamines and, in resistant cases, narrowband ultraviolet B or short-course systemic corticosteroid.
reference.pathophysiology: Atopic eruption of pregnancy reflects a flare of atopic dermatitis-type disease driven by the physiological immunological changes of pregnancy. Gestation promotes a shift from T-helper-1 towards T-helper-2 cytokine predominance with reduced production of interferon-gamma and interleukin-2 and increased interleukin-4 and interleukin-10, an environment that favours the atopic phenotype and skin barrier-related pruritus. In a predisposed woman this unmasks or exacerbates eczematous and papular skin changes. The condition is not autoimmune and has no basement membrane zone antibody, distinguishing it from pemphigoid gestationis, and there is no hepatobiliary disturbance as seen in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
additionalDifferentials: prurigo of pregnancy (now within this spectrum)
additionalInvestigations: serum bile acids and liver function tests to exclude intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
total and specific serum IgE (often elevated)
direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin (negative, to exclude pemphigoid gestationis)
skin biopsy in atypical cases (spongiotic dermatitis or non-specific changes)
skin swabs if secondary bacterial or eczema herpeticum infection is suspected
skin scrapings for scabies when clinically indicated
redFlags: generalised pruritus without primary lesions plus raised bile acids indicating intrahepatic cholestasis with fetal risk
tense blisters or periumbilical involvement suggesting pemphigoid gestationis
rapidly worsening painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions suggesting eczema herpeticum
spreading erythema, weeping and crusting indicating secondary bacterial infection
systemic symptoms or mucosal involvement suggesting an alternative severe drug or infective reaction
reference.prognosis: Benign for mother and fetus with a good response to topical treatment, though flares may persist through pregnancy and settle after delivery. Recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is common owing to the underlying atopic predisposition.
pitfalls: Failing to check bile acids and missing intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy in a woman presenting with itch.
Missing eczema herpeticum in an atopic flare, a dermatological emergency requiring prompt antiviral therapy.
Withholding topical corticosteroids through unfounded fear of harm and leaving disease undertreated.
Mistaking widespread eczematous AEP for a drug eruption and stopping essential medication unnecessarily.
Not recognising that prurigo and pruritic folliculitis of pregnancy fall within this spectrum, causing diagnostic confusion.
